title: Quant aptitude: percentages & profit
examples: How do I calculate the final price after several discounts?
What is the quickest way to find the overall percentage change?
Can you show me an example involving cost price and selling price?

explain.say: Today we are learning about successive percentage changes in profit.
When you have successive percentage changes you multiply the factors.
For example a ten percent increase followed by a twenty percent decrease is calculated like this.
The combined effect is found by multiplying these individual multipliers together.
If an item increases by twenty percent then decreases by ten percent the overall change is found by multiplying.
In a real shop sale if the price drops by fifteen percent and then another ten percent discount is applied it is successive change.

faq.q: When should I use this successive percentage method?
faq.a: Use this when a value changes by one percentage, and then the new value changes by another percentage.
asks: Does this apply to profit and loss?

faq.q: Do I always use the multiplier method?
faq.a: The multiplier method is the fastest way to calculate the net effect of sequential changes.
asks: Is there a formula for this?
Can I just add the percentages?

faq.q: If the percentage change is negative what do I do?
faq.a: A negative percentage change means a decrease, so you use a multiplier less than one.

faq.q: Does the order of changes matter?
faq.a: Yes the order matters greatly because the second percentage is calculated on the new, changed amount.

faq.q: What is the difference between successive change and simple change?
faq.a: Simple change applies the percentage to the original amount every time, but successive change applies it to the new amount.

facts: A percentage increase of p percent uses a multiplier of (1 + p/100).
A percentage decrease of p percent uses a multiplier of (1 - p/100).
The overall change from successive percentages is found by multiplying the individual multipliers.
If the changes are equal and opposite, the net change is not zero unless the percentages are zero.

quiz.say: A value increases by twenty percent and then increases by another ten percent. What is the total multiplier?
quiz.why: You multiply 1.2 by 1.1 because the second ten percent increase is on the already increased value.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you only considered the first change and ignored the second ten percent increase.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you added the percentages (20 + 10 = 30%) and then incorrectly multiplied by 10.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you only applied the second change to the original value, ignoring the first increase.

quiz.say: A price is first reduced by twenty percent and then reduced by another twenty percent. What is the final multiplier?
quiz.why: The second twenty percent reduction is calculated on the price already reduced by the first twenty percent.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you added the percentages (20 + 20 = 40%) and then incorrectly subtracted from one.
wrong.1: This is wrong because you treated the changes as simple subtraction from one, ignoring the compounding effect.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you incorrectly calculated the total reduction as 40% off the original value.

quiz.say: If a quantity increases by twenty percent and then decreases by twenty percent, what is the overall change multiplier?
quiz.why: The multiplier is 1.2 multiplied by 0.8 because the decrease is applied to the increased amount.

wrong.1: This is wrong because you assumed the changes cancel out, but the second change is on a larger base.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you only calculated the difference between the two percentages.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you added the percentages (20 + 20) and then incorrectly calculated the net change.
